steps.action:
# The Last Light

Every night, Edmund climbed 127 steps.

He had counted them thirty years ago on his first night, and he had never stopped counting since. It was the kind of habit that kept a man honest about where he was going.

The light at the top of Carrow Point had been his entire world since his wife passed. People in town called him lonely. He called it chosen.

On a Tuesday in November, a storm rolled in that bent the pine trees sideways. Edmund climbed his 127 steps, lit the lamp, and watched the black water below churn itself white.

Just after midnight, he saw it — a small vessel, maybe forty feet, drifting too close to the rocks at Shepherd's Jaw. He grabbed his radio. Nothing. He fired his signal flare. Nothing.

So he did the only thing he could. He turned the lamp to its highest rotation, the fastest it had spun in years, and he pressed his hands against the warm glass housing and willed that boat to see it.

It turned.

Slowly, desperately, but it turned.

He never found out who was on that boat. No one came to thank him. The storm moved on and the sea went quiet and Tuesday became Wednesday the way it always did.

Edmund climbed back down his 127 steps, put the kettle on, and decided that was enough.

It was always enough.
